cards.text: A name is really a word with no meaning. Omar does not describe anything, so you give it a picture of your own. Later this year you will do the same with words from other languages, and with words that mean nothing at all. It is the same job.

Before you picture anything, say the new word out loud, twice. The picture should match the sound, not the spelling. Many words come with a say-it spelling, like kee-TAH-boo for kitabu. The capital letters show where the stress falls. It is only a rough guide, so listen to a native speaker too when you can.

Some words have no English hook at all. For those, cut the sound into pieces, one piece per syllable, and give each piece a sound-alike: chakula becomes chalk plus cooler. Then join the pieces in one small scene that acts on the meaning. This week you also practise words from the old tongue of Veyra. They are invented and mean nothing to anyone yet, so they are pure sound, which makes them a fair test.

This week you practise Spanish both ways round. First you see the Spanish word and give the meaning. Then you see the meaning and give the Spanish word. The second way is harder, and doing the harder version is exactly what makes a word stay. Accents are not needed when you type.

Look-alike words blur the most: in Turkish, kapı is a door and kapak is a lid. When two words are close, make them look different in your mind. Give each its own colour, or put them in two different rooms of your palace.

One drill this week has words with no meaning at all. You only keep the sound. Say each word, cut it into syllables, give each syllable a quick sound-alike, and string them into one tiny scene. This is the same skill you use for a stranger's name or a word you hear once on a trip.

Spanish sorts nouns into two groups, el and la. Make the group part of the picture: every el word is on fire, every la word is made of ice. Then the article comes back with the word. Watch for surprises like la mano, the hand, which is a la word even though it ends in o.

Short phrases work like little chains. Give each word a picture and link them in order, then picture where you would say it: asking for the bill, finding the bathroom, greeting someone in the morning. The place helps the phrase come back when you need it.

From this week, each full session has a real-life scene: a neighbour's shopping list, directions from a stranger, a voicemail with a number in it. You use the same tools, but the questions come the way life asks them: what came after the eggs, which way at the fountain. The next day, the same scene comes back with different questions.

This week the scenes arrive with no label. Before you see the material, pick the tool yourself. Ask four quick questions: is it in order? Is it numbers? Is it a person? Is it a foreign word? Order means a story chain or a palace. Numbers mean the Major System. A person means face and name. A foreign word means a keyword. Choosing well is a skill of its own, and it is the one you will use most outside this game.

After a scene you can make a plan for real life: when I walk into a shop, I will put the list in my palace. If you like, type a few real things you need to keep this week. Mnemos will ask for them tomorrow and again in a week. Plans that name a moment and a tool are much more likely to happen than good intentions.

Ever heard a great joke and lost it by the next morning? A joke is a pair: the setup and the punchline. The punchline usually turns on one word. Find that word, picture it, and link it to the main picture in the setup. What has keys but cannot open a door? Picture a huge piano with a ring of door keys for its keys. Now the punchline comes back with the question.

A year is just a four-digit number with a story attached. Split it into two Major System pictures and put them inside the event. 1066 is 10, toes, and 66, a judge: picture a judge stamping on soldiers' toes at Hastings. 1492 is 14, a tyre, and 92, a bone: a tyre and a bone tied to the front of Columbus's ship. The stranger the scene, the longer the year stays.

Surprising facts are easy to enjoy and hard to keep. Two things help. First, picture the surprise itself: an octopus with three hearts beating in a row like drums. Second, read the reason. A fact that makes sense hooks onto things you already know, so it has more ways back.

A labelled diagram is a small palace you can see. Walk it in the same order every time, top to bottom or round like a clock. At each spot, give the label a picture that sits right there: a stigma on top of the flower becomes a sticky stamp, the style below it a stylish pole. When the labels are gone, walk the same path and the pictures are still sitting in their places.

Formulas look like code, which is why they slip away. Two steps make them stay. First, know what each letter means: in F = m a, F is force, m is mass and a is acceleration. Then give each symbol a fixed picture you use every time: π is a pie, a small 2 is a swan, a fraction bar is a table top, an equals sign is a bridge. Now F = m a is a Farmer on a bridge carrying a Mule that Accelerates. Keep the same symbol pictures for life and every new formula gets quicker.

Chemical formulas are short words made of element symbols. Say them aloud as a word: NaCl is na-cul, H₂O is two hydrogens holding one oxygen like a balloon between two children. The small numbers tell you how many of each, so picture that many.
